Socrates
sŏk´ra-tēz
n. (Athenian philosopher, c. 470–399 BC, executed by his own city for impiety and corrupting the youth)
Greek Sokrates. He wrote nothing; what survives is Plato's and Xenophon's report of him. Calvin cites him as the best the pagan world produced, and uses him to mark the limit of that world.

Biblical Definition

Socrates is not named in Scripture; his city and his method are. Paul met the philosophers of Athens in the market daily as Socrates had (Act 17:17–18), and was accused, as Socrates was, of setting forth strange gods. Scripture grants the pagan mind a real light: “that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them” (Rom 1:19). It also names where that light stops: “professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom 1:22); “the world by wisdom knew not God” (1Co 1:21). And it puts the true starting point elsewhere: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Socratic as pertaining to Socrates, his philosophy or method of teaching; the Socratic method being that of teaching by a series of questions and inductions.

expand to see more

SOCRATIC, SOCRATICAL, a. Pertaining to Socrates, the Grecian sage, or to his manner of teaching and philosophizing.

The Socratic method of reasoning and instruction was by questions, the answers to which led on the disputant to the conclusion sought.

SOCRATISM, n. The doctrines or philosophy of Socrates.

Key Scripture

Act 17:18 — "Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection."

Rom 1:19 — "Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them."

Rom 1:22 — "Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools,"

1Co 1:21 — "For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe."

Pro 9:10 — "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding."

Modern Corruption

The best pagan is made into an honorary Christian, or dismissed as though he saw nothing at all.

expand to see more

Socrates is the standing test case for the doctrine of common grace, and the church has erred in both directions about him. Some of the fathers made him a Christian before Christ; some of the Reformers' successors would allow him nothing. The Reformed position holds two things at once. He genuinely saw something — that the unexamined life is not worth living, that it is better to suffer wrong than to do it, that a man's soul is what he ought to care for — and Romans 1:19 says such sight is not accidental, since God shewed it unto them. That is common grace, and it is God's gift whoever receives it.

The limit is equally firm and it is not that his ethics were poor. Romans 1:22 does not say they became foolish in their reasoning; it says professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, and the folly named in the following verses is worship misdirected. A man may reason beautifully about the good and still not know whom to thank, and 1 Corinthians 1:21 states the outcome as a settled fact of history: after all of it, the world by wisdom knew not God. The failure was not intellectual capacity but a knowledge that requires being told.

Proverbs 9:10 puts the two together with a word that does the work: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Not its capstone, added after the philosophy is finished, but the point from which understanding starts. Which is why a Christian may read Socrates with real profit and must not read him as a preparation that the gospel then completes. Athens produced the finest questions the unaided mind has asked. It did not produce the answer, and Paul had to bring it to them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sophia (G4678), wisdom; moraino (G3471), to become foolish; Hebrew yirath YHWH (H3374), the fear of the LORD; reshith (H7225), beginning.

Hebrew yirath YHWH reshith chokmah (H3374, H7225) — the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; Proverbs 9:10, 1:7, Psalm 111:10.

Greek emoranthesan (G3471) — they became fools; Romans 1:22.

Greek dia tes sophias (G4678) — by wisdom; 1 Corinthians 1:21.

Usage

"“That which may be known of God is manifest in them” — and he saw some of it."

"“Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” — not in reasoning, in worship."

"“The beginning of wisdom” — the beginning, not the capstone."
